key_insight: A first-principles statistical model shows that multi-scale "semantic chunking" in natural language explains why printed English has an entropy rate near ~1 bit/character, accounting for roughly 80% redundancy relative to random text.
problem_solved: Explains the long-standing puzzle of why natural language has such low entropy (high redundancy) by providing a mechanistic account of multi-scale structure rather than treating redundancy as an empirical artifact.
method: Propose a statistical model that explicitly encodes hierarchical, multi-scale semantic chunking in text generation.
Derive and/or simulate the entropy rate produced by this model to match observed ~1 bit/character estimates for printed English.
Analyze how chunk sizes and dependencies across scales contribute to overall redundancy.
impact: Provides a principled explanation of language redundancy that can guide more efficient text compression, inform inductive biases for language models, and improve interpretability of multi-scale representations in NLP systems.
visual_elements: Entropy bar chart: compare entropy per character for random text (5 bits), printed English (~1 bit), and model prediction.
Hierarchical chunking diagram: nested boxes or tree showing semantic chunks at multiple scales aggregating into sentences/paragraphs.
Flowchart of the model: how chunk generation and inter-chunk dependencies produce text and reduce entropy.
Heatmap or curve: contribution of chunk size / scale to total redundancy (percent redundancy vs. scale).
paper_title: Semantic Chunking and the Entropy of Natural Language
paper_authors: Weishun Zhong, Doron Sivan, Tankut Can, Mikhail Katkov, Misha Tsodyks
